title: 3Sum
space_complexity: O(1) auxiliary (excluding the O(log N) sort stack and the output); the set-based first attempt was O(N)
revisit_reason: Struggled with the hashmap approach first; want to re-derive the two-pointer + in-place dedup solution from scratch and internalize why hashmap is painful here.
takeaways: Sorting an array is a powerful pre-processing step for problems involving combinations, order, or duplicate handling.
The 'N-Sum' problem (e.g., 3Sum, 4Sum) can often be solved by reducing it to an (N-1)-Sum problem by fixing one element and applying iteration or recursion.
The Two Pointers technique is highly effective for finding pairs with a target sum in a sorted array and for skipping duplicate elements.
Careful duplicate handling is essential at all levels (for the fixed element and the two-pointer elements) to ensure the solution set contains only unique triplets.

Sorting turns the dedup problem from hard (hashmap: dedup unordered triplets) into trivial (skip equal neighbours), which is why the O(N^2) sorted approach beats the hashmap attempt despite the same time class.
Bounds check before the array read: write `while (l < r && nums[l] == nums[l-1])`, not the reverse, so the pointer guard short-circuits before a possible out-of-range access.
